kp.k: Accumulated capital structures opportunities and reproduces advantage
kp.d: Bourdieu presents a theoretical account of the social world as accumulated history: capital takes time to acquire, persists, and shapes the possibilities available to agents. His framework challenges representations of competition as a sequence of independent opportunities unconstrained by inheritance or prior accumulation. The essay does not discuss AI or legal services.
qs: The social world is accumulated history

kp.k: Capital has economic, cultural, and social forms
kp.d: Bourdieu distinguishes economic capital, directly convertible into money and institutionalized through property rights; cultural capital, conditionally convertible into economic capital and institutionalized through educational qualifications; and social capital, grounded in connections and obligations. Their efficacy and conversion depend on the field and the transformations required, rather than on simple equivalence with money.

kp.k: Narrow economics obscures interested, apparently disinterested practices
kp.d: Bourdieu argues that restricting economic analysis to monetary profit and mercantile exchange defines other exchanges as disinterested, concealing their material and symbolic returns. He advocates an account of practices that encompasses multiple forms of capital without reducing their distinctive effects to monetary transactions.

kp.k: Cultural capital challenges natural-ability explanations of educational inequality
kp.d: Bourdieu describes cultural capital as a hypothesis developed through research to explain class differences in scholastic achievement. He criticizes human-capital approaches for neglecting family transmission and the wider system of educational and reproduction strategies, and argues that ability itself reflects prior investments of time and cultural capital. The essay does not provide a sample size or quantitative estimate for these claims.

kp.k: Embodied capital requires personal acquisition and time
kp.d: Embodied cultural capital consists of lasting dispositions acquired through incorporation and work on oneself. Bourdieu argues that its acquisition cannot be delegated and that acquisition time should include early domestic education, not merely schooling. Because it becomes part of the person, its transfer and exploitation differ from the transfer of money or property.

kp.k: Family resources support cumulative cultural advantage
kp.d: Bourdieu argues that family cultural capital affects how early accumulation begins and how readily further cultural resources can be appropriated. Economic resources support prolonged acquisition by providing time free from economic necessity, purchasing others' time, and delaying entry into the labor market. These mechanisms make cultural inheritance an especially concealed form of intergenerational advantage.

kp.k: Owning cultural goods differs from mastering their use
kp.d: Objectified cultural capital includes material objects such as writings, paintings, instruments, and machines. Their legal ownership can be transferred, but effective symbolic appropriation requires embodied cultural capital. Consequently, owners of productive equipment need relevant competence themselves or access to the services of those possessing it.

kp.k: Technical specialists occupy an ambiguous class position
kp.d: Bourdieu describes executives and engineers as ambiguous because they lack economic ownership of the means of production yet derive profits from possessing specialized cultural capital. He conditionally suggests that increasing cultural capital incorporated into production could strengthen such workers collectively, while emphasizing that economic-capital holders can counteract this by setting them in competition with one another.

kp.k: Qualifications institutionalize competence but cannot guarantee stable returns
kp.d: Academic qualifications give cultural competence officially recognized status distinct from competence that must continually prove itself. They enable comparison and substitution among holders and help establish economic conversion rates. Nevertheless, returns depend on scarcity and changing opportunities; educational investment can yield less than expected. Bourdieu further argues that social connections and the standing of the bearer affect the value of credentials.

kp.k: Social capital depends on mobilizable connections and resources
kp.d: Bourdieu defines social capital through durable relationships of mutual recognition and group membership. Its volume depends on the connections an agent can mobilize and the resources those contacts possess. It is not reducible to an individual's economic or cultural holdings, but its formation presupposes some shared properties and it multiplies the efficacy of those holdings.

kp.k: Networks require maintenance and reproduce group boundaries
kp.d: Relationships are produced through continuing investment, exchanges, and institutional practices rather than being permanently secured by kinship or proximity. Sociability consumes time, energy, and economic resources and requires acquired competence. Select schools, clubs, and organized occasions bring relatively homogeneous people together, while exchanges reaffirm membership boundaries. Established names and inherited connections make subsequent network accumulation more productive.

kp.k: Delegation concentrates collective power and risks appropriation
kp.d: Groups concentrate social capital in representatives who can act with power exceeding their personal contribution. This enables collective action across space and time but creates the possibility that representatives appropriate the group's capital or substitute themselves for it. Bourdieu treats identification with leaders as a possibility inherent in representation, not simply an incidental misuse.

kp.k: Capital conversion entails labor, delay, and possible losses
kp.d: Bourdieu posits economic capital as the root of the other forms while rejecting the idea that this exhausts their specific effects. Conversion requires work and time: relationships must often be cultivated before they are useful, and cultural acquisition requires sustained investment. Reproduction strategies seek conversions with lower costs and losses, subject to existing power relations and differences in transmissibility.

kp.k: Symbolic recognition need not involve conscious calculation
kp.d: Symbolic capital concerns capital recognized through socially constituted perceptions, including misrecognition of its basis. Bourdieu cautions against treating investment strategies as necessarily cynical or consciously profit-seeking: sincere commitments and apparently disinterested conduct can correspond to objective interests. Habitus can orient choices without explicit calculation.

kp.k: Cultural advantage depends on unequal access and valuation
kp.d: Bourdieu qualifies the capital concept by arguing that embodied culture does not confer exclusive advantages where access to cultural appropriation is equally distributed. He also distinguishes educational judgments from judgments of intrinsic worth: dispositions devalued in education may be valued in other markets, including relationships within a class.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bourdieu advances cross-domain claims about how economic, cultural and social capital produce unequal educational achievement, economic returns and the reproduction of social advantage; he makes no claims about AI or legal services.
pts.d: Bourdieu argues that academic success reflects the unequal distribution and domestic transmission of cultural capital rather than simply natural aptitude or monetary educational investment. Economic resources support cultural acquisition by financing time free from economic necessity. Ownership of cultural objects or machinery does not itself supply the embodied competence necessary to use them: owners must possess that competence or obtain the services of its holders. Academic qualifications institutionalize recognition of competence and facilitate its conversion into economic returns, but those returns depend on scarcity and can fall below expectations. Social capital provides access to collective resources and multiplies the effects of a person's other capital. Networks require investment and maintenance rather than arising automatically. Conversion among forms of capital helps reproduce social positions, but entails time, costs and possible losses. These are Bourdieu's sociological arguments, not predictions about technological change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is primarily theoretical synthesis informed by research, supported by institutional examples and engagement with existing scholarship, rather than quantified tests reported in this chapter.
pts.d: Bourdieu presents cultural capital as a theoretical hypothesis developed during research into unequal scholastic achievement. He critiques Becker's human-capital approach for overlooking domestic cultural transmission and nonmonetary investments and returns. Illustrations include differences between legal ownership and competent use of cultural goods, competitive recruitment examinations, educational credentials, elite clubs, family networks and the delegation of group resources to representatives. References include Becker, Bourdieu's work on institution rites, Breton and Grassby. The chapter does not report a sample, statistical effect estimate or experimental test establishing the magnitude of its central mechanisms. Bourdieu explicitly acknowledges the risk of schematic conceptual exposition. The translator's note about the French relationship between qualifications, rank and remuneration should not be treated as a separate finding by Bourdieu.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The mechanisms operate through prolonged acquisition, relationship maintenance and intergenerational transmission, with returns conditional on the structure of the relevant field.
pts.d: Published in English in 1986, the chapter offers no dated forecast. Embodied cultural capital requires personal acquisition over time and cannot be transferred instantaneously like money or property rights. Families with substantial cultural resources can begin transmission early; economic resources determine how long acquisition and schooling can continue without entry into paid work. Social connections must generally be established before they are needed, and maintaining them consumes time and energy. Educational investment may pay off only over a long period, if at all. Credential returns depend on scarcity and changing conversion rates between cultural and economic capital. Cultural competence confers exclusive advantages where access to it is unequally distributed, rather than universally. Bourdieu also qualifies the suggestion that increasing technical knowledge in production strengthens its holders: owners of economic capital can counter this by making holders of cultural capital compete with one another. Reproduction strategies change when direct inheritance is constrained, increasing the importance of less visible transmission.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are children and families across social classes, qualification holders, owners and skilled employees, and members and representatives of resource-bearing networks.
pts.d: Children in culturally and economically advantaged families obtain an earlier start and more time for cultural acquisition; children lacking those resources face unequal conditions of educational competition. Qualification holders receive institutional recognition but do not necessarily obtain equivalent returns from equivalent credentials, because their other resources and connections matter. Economic owners depend on embodied expertise to use technically sophisticated productive assets. Executives and engineers occupy an ambiguous position: they sell skilled services without necessarily owning the productive assets, yet derive returns from their own cultural capital. Members of prestigious families, schools and clubs benefit from collective backing and useful relationships, with greater benefits where contacts possess more capital. Representatives can mobilize a group's collective capital but may also appropriate or exercise that power against the group. Dominant families can diversify their reproduction strategies and use economic and social resources to offset unfavorable educational outcomes.
